item.title: Losing our progress to extreme heat. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
We are shocked to learn that, as per a study by the International Institute for Environment and Development (IIED) and the Ovibashi Karmi Unnayan Program (OKUP), informal workers collectively lose an estimated Tk50,630 crore in wages annually because of extreme heat.
This is a staggering economic blow that is equivalent to 0.91% of GDP. To dismiss it as a distant climate threat would be a grave error—it is a present economic crisis.
With outdoor workers missing up to 24 days of work each year due to unbearable temperatures, while indoor workers are also losing about 14 days too, we must remember that these are people who already earn below a living wage, and every lost day pushes them deeper into financial insecurity.
While we cannot control the weather, we can reiterate that such extreme heat is as a result of climate change, and this global warming has been caused by the developed world.
That they continue to not do their part in supporting developing nations such as ours suffering disproportionately from this crisis is among the greatest global failures of our time.
With that said, Bangladesh too must implement heat‑response measures immediately, from investing in cooling centers to better heat‑resilient housing upgrades for informal settlements.
There is also the need for a more humanitarian approach to the work itself, with mandatory rest breaks and shade for outdoor workers and the necessary medical support for workers exposed to chronic heat.
Aspirations of becoming an equitable nation will never be realized if we fail to recognize that the majority of our working population continue to suffer and are unable to work to their full potential.

item.title: Reviving jute means supporting farmers. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
For years now, we have been speaking of the potential of jute, and for the need to support its production.
To that end, that farmers are struggling to receive fair prices for jute after a year of promising yield is disappointing.
Jute is not just another crop. It is a national asset, a symbol of rural livelihoods, and a sector with enormous potential for value-added exports.
Yet, the farmers who sustain this “golden fiber" continue to face a market that does not value their work.
High production costs, exploitative middlemen, and inconsistent government procurement have created a situation where farmers bear all the risks but receive none of the rewards.
The contradiction is glaring. Bangladesh speaks proudly of diversifying exports, expanding jute‑based industries, and promoting eco‑friendly alternatives to plastic.
Yet, these ambitions ring hollow when farmers in major producing districts cannot earn enough to survive.
It goes without saying that a sector cannot thrive when its foundation is collapsing, and the authorities concerned should treat this moment with urgency.
Farmers need fair and predictable prices, not seasonal fluctuations that leave them vulnerable, and need protection from syndicates that manipulate the market. Supporting this industry also means ensuring farmers have access to storage and transport so they are not forced to sell at distress rates.
Above all, they need a policy framework that recognizes jute for its present and future importance and supports it accordingly.
If Bangladesh wants jute to remain a pillar of its rural economy and export future, it must ensure that the people who grow it are not left behind.

item.title: Two statutes older than the internet are setting startup policy. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Somewhere in Dhaka right now, a software company with paying customers in 40 countries is being incorporated in Wyoming. The founder is Bangladeshi, the engineers are Bangladeshi, and the salaries will be paid in taka. The company will be American, and making it so costs about $500.
The reason is Stripe. It does not support Bangladesh, and neither does PayPal in any form that lets a business here receive and withdraw revenue. Sell software to the world, and you need a payments provider, and every serious one requires an entity incorporated in a country on its list.
A private company's compliance list has become the most influential piece of corporate policy affecting Bangladeshi start-ups. That should trouble us more than the funding chart does.
We treat incorporation as a tax question. It is a question of what a company may sign.
A Bangladeshi private limited company cannot hold a Stripe account. It cannot issue a SAFE or a convertible note, neither of which has statutory recognition under the Companies Act 1994.
It cannot give a fund a liquidation preference backed by a forum that resolves in months. It cannot be acquired by a foreign buyer without prior Bangladesh Bank approval on transfer of control.
Each of those is a contract, and a Delaware or Singapore entity signs all of them on a Tuesday. Founders know the offshore parent will be required eventually and that doing it later is expensive, so they do it first.
The tax explanation has run out.
The Finance Act 2026 rebuilt the startup regime. A registered startup under Tk 100 crore in turnover gets a nine-year growth period, a turnover tax cut to zero across it, a loss carry-forward that survives changes in shareholding, and VAT exemption until June 2035.
For a loss-making early-stage company, the tax position in Dhaka is now at least as good as Singapore's. FEID Circular 1 of March 2026 then lets banks clear repatriation of share proceeds up to Tk 100 crore without central bank sign-off, 10 times the old ceiling, in five days.
These are serious reforms, and the people behind them deserve credit. But founders kept incorporating abroad through both.
One condition runs through the package. A startup, for these purposes, is a company incorporated under the Companies Act 1994. The relief reaches only the founders who stayed and answers a question they were not asking.
Two groups leave for unrelated reasons. Venture-track companies flip at the first institutional round, because a fund requires an offshore parent before it wires.
Bootstrapped software companies flip in week one, because a payments provider requires a listed-country entity before it processes.
The second group is larger by headcount and invisible by construction.
When we read that start-ups raised six million dollars in the first half of 2026 and conclude the ecosystem is finished, we are reading a register of who chose Bangladeshi paperwork.
Foreign exchange is governed by an Act from 1947, written before the country existed. Companies are governed by an Act from 1994, written before the commercial internet.
Circulars have patched around both for two years, and a circular cannot create an instrument the underlying Act does not contemplate.
The July 2025 Share Swap circular lets shareholders swap operating company shares for offshore holdco shares with no capital leaving Bangladesh: Useful, and a bridge built toward the offshore parent rather than a removal of the reason to want one.
A startup schedule inside the Companies Act would do most of the work. Statutory recognition for convertible instruments. Primacy for shareholder agreements over articles, so preferences and drag-along bind as written.
A commercial forum with a fixed clock, because investors are pricing years and months, would change that price. And publication of Bangladeshi-founded funding beside Bangladesh-domiciled funding, because a country cannot tax what its statistics decline to see.
I have raised money into a Bangladeshi cap table and into a Singapore one. The difference was never conviction about where to build. It was that one legal vocabulary had a word for the instrument the investor held.
Six million dollars is a number about paperwork. The companies are here.
Hussain M Elius co-founded Pathao and founded Wind. He is the author of "Moving Bangladesh: The Origin Story of Pathao."

item.title: The economic impact of diabetes. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Diabetes is a chronic condition that occurs when the body cannot produce enough or effectively use insulin. Insulin is a hormone produced by the pancreas that allows glucose from food to enter the body’s cells, where it is converted into energy needed by muscles and tissues to function.
As a result, a person with diabetes does not absorb glucose properly, and glucose stays circulating in the blood (hyperglycemia), damaging tissues over time. This damage leads to life-threatening health complications.
According to the Diabetes Atlas published by the International Diabetic Federation, as of 2024, 589 million adults (20-79 years) are living with diabetes worldwide.
Diabetes imposes a large economic burden on any national healthcare system; estimated figures show healthcare expenditures on diabetes accounted for 11.8% of the total healthcare expenditure in the world in 2025.
About 95% of the countries spend 5% or more of their total healthcare dollars on diabetes. Global health expenditures to prevent and treat diabetes and its complications surpassed $376 billion in 2010, and by 2030, this number will be close to $500bn.
Research results show that there remains a large disparity in healthcare spending on diabetes between regions and countries. More than 80% of the global expenditures on diabetes are made in the world's most economically rich countries, not in the low- and middle-income countries where 80% of people with diabetes live.
Recent studies drew three major conclusions on the overall economic impact of diabetes
First , diabetes imposes a large financial burden on people with diabetes and their families. The size of this burden depends on their economic status and the social insurance policies of the countries in which they live.
Individuals with diabetes and their families in developing countries pay a larger share of the expenditure because of the poorer organized systems of medical care insurance and/or lack of governmental provision of medical services.
In the poorest countries, people with diabetes and their families bear almost the whole cost of whatever medical care they can afford.
Second , at the societal level, diabetes leads to loss in productivity and economic growth. It is estimated that the US economy lost over $100bn as a result of lost earnings due to lost workdays, restricted activity days, lower productivity at work, mortality, and permanent disability caused by diabetes.
Such losses are even larger in poorer countries relative to GDP because premature death due to diabetes occurs at much younger ages.
Finally , the largest economic burden caused by diabetes is the monetary value associated with disability and loss of life as a result of the disease itself and its related complications, including heart, kidney, eye, and foot disease.
Economists have used different methods to value disability and loss of life associated with diseases, and the most appropriate method is still debated. Yet, no matter what method is used, it is very likely the economic burden that is measured by the monetary value associated with this disability and loss of life would be far larger than the estimated economic burden using measures described above.
Most people with diabetes live in less developed regions of the world. Even in the region with the lowest prevalence (Africa), according to the IDF Diabetes Atlas (9th Edition) released for 2019, diabetes was responsible for an estimated 366,200 deaths in the IDF Africa Region.
Diabetes has reached epidemic proportions worldwide. Every year, more people are diagnosed with diabetes, yet there are still many (more than 50%) people who have diabetes and do not know it. A small survey in Bangladesh indicated that the prevalence of diabetes in Bangladesh in populations aged over 15 years is between 2% and 5%. This type of similarity is also found in most of the underdeveloped countries.
Since diabetes is a life-long and non-episodic disease that affects many other organs of the body, a comprehensive and good pathological support-based treatment is needed to manage it.
Dr Muhammad Abdul Mazid is formerly secretary and chairman, NBR, and National Council Member of the Diabetic Association of Bangladesh.

Bangladesh hospital wards crowded as measles toll nears grim 1,000-child mark. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Bangladesh’s deadliest measles outbreak in decades is nearing the grim milestone of 1,000 child deaths, as a devastating epidemic sweeps through the country and crowded hospital wards fill with struggling babies.

Cries of sick children and the hiss of oxygen machines fill the air at Dhaka’s Shishu Hospital, where Rima Akter keeps a vigil beside her nine-month-old son.

“Just an hour ago, a child died, and they wheeled him out in front of us,” 30-year-old Akter told AFP on Thursday.

“We saw two children die today.”

Akter’s son Sabit Haque is one of scores filling the children’s hospital’s measles wards.

At least 986 children have died since March, while suspected and confirmed cases have surged past 180,000, according to the latest health ministry figures.

Measles is highly contagious, spreading through coughs and sneezes, and has no specific treatment once caught.

Complications can include brain swelling and severe breathing problems.

Although anyone can catch the disease, young children are particularly vulnerable.

The South Asian nation of 170 million has rolled out a mass vaccination drive to combat the outbreak, but case numbers continue to climb.

More than 1,000 suspected cases are reported daily.

‘Very weak’

“I’ve been running to and from multiple hospitals since July to get my son the proper treatment,” said Sanjana Islam Modina, 19, cradling her six-month-old son Ayan, who has an oxygen tube fixed to his nose.

Small dark spots covered Ayan’s head, fading from the angry red rash left by measles.

He was first admitted to hospital with pneumonia in July, then contracted measles before finally securing a bed at the capital’s specialised children’s hospital in mid-August.

Ayan spent 15 days in intensive care, before improving enough to return to the dedicated measles ward.

The hospital currently has 101 children admitted with suspected or confirmed measles.

“His lungs were already very weak from the pneumonia, then with measles his breathing was affected more,” Modina told AFP, while trying to soothe her wailing baby.

“He’s been on oxygen constantly for the last five days.”

Most cases recorded in Bangladesh during the current outbreak have been among children aged between six months and five years.

Doctors say many of the children arriving at hospital are already critically ill, with malnutrition further weakening their ability to fight the virus.

Ayan has also been diagnosed as malnourished.

“The doctors gave my son a special milk specifically designed for malnourished children,” said Modina, wiping sweat from his tiny forehead.

‘Devastating’

The outbreak has exposed gaps in Bangladesh’s efforts to protect its youngest.

SM Ziauddin Hyder, special assistant to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman for health, called the outbreak “devastating”.

Bangladesh had previously made major advances in vaccination against infectious diseases, but a measles drive planned for 2024 was delayed by the uprising that toppled former prime minister Sheikh Hasina.

Workers’ strikes and political instability delayed a 2025 campaign.

The country has since rolled out a mass vaccination drive to combat the outbreak, but the number of cases continues to climb.

“There was a gap of a significant number of children missing the doses,” Hyder said.

“Healthcare workers… are vaccinating these children to close the gap.”

Mahmudur Rahman, an epidemiologist and former director of the Institute of Epidemiology, Disease Control and Research (IEDCR), said Bangladesh should consider a broader vaccination campaign to contain the outbreak.

Rahman said public awareness was also crucial, stressing preventive measures including isolating infected children, handwashing and the use of masks by caregivers.

Worried mother Akter needs no reminder of how quickly the sickness can spread.

“We are aware of how contagious this disease is; our son was first admitted for bronchitis,” she said.

“After being released, we had to come back for measles.”

item.title: Turning waste into opportunity. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The scale of Bangladesh’s tannery waste problem is troubling, but there is certainly an economic opportunity hidden within it that we would be remiss to overlook.
Experts estimate that properly processing tannery waste and turning it into value-added products could generate an additional Tk2,000-3,000 crore in annual revenue.
This is precisely the kind of opportunity Bangladesh should be pursuing: One that can simultaneously address an environmental crisis, create new industries, generate employment, and also strengthen an important export sector.
For years, tannery waste has largely been treated as something to be disposed of rather than a resource to be recovered, and the consequences have been severe: Poorly managed waste has contributed to pollution around the Savar Tannery Industrial Estate, adding further pressure to already struggling waterways.
At a time when our rivers are being overwhelmed by industrial and other forms of waste, continuing with such a linear approach is simply unsustainable.
Yet, the materials currently being discarded have considerable potential.
Collagen-rich waste can be converted into products such as gelatin, industrial tallow, bio-fertilizer, and leather board, while chrome shavings and other by-products can have applications ranging from capsule shells to other industrial materials.
Even treatment-plant sludge has reportedly been used to produce tiles and bricks.
What is needed now is a serious transition towards a circular economy -- which will require investment in waste-processing facilities, green financing, appropriate incentives, research and development, and stronger links between waste processors and markets.
The government must also address the industry's environmental compliance problems. Environmental protection and economic growth should not be presented as opposing objectives; in this case, they can reinforce one another.
The opportunity before us is clear: Instead of allowing tannery waste to become another burden on our rivers and communities, Bangladesh should turn it into a valuable resource. Doing so would be good environmental policy -- and smart economics.

Feeding our future. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
We agree with the State Minister for Primary and Mass Education Bobby Hajjaj that providing midday meals to schoolchildren must be viewed as a right rather than an act of charity.
His remarks come at an important time, as Bangladesh seeks to improve both access to and the quality of primary education.
A child cannot be expected to concentrate on lessons while hungry, and for many children from low-income households, the meal received at school may be the most integral part of their daily nutrition.
A properly designed and implemented school feeding program can, therefore, do much more than put food on a plate: It can improve attendance, concentration, learning outcomes, and ultimately a child's prospects in life.
This is particularly important if the government's stated ambition is to ensure that no child remains out of school, and that every child receives a proper education.
Investment in classrooms and textbooks will only go so far if children arrive at school hungry or leave because their families cannot afford to meet their basic needs.
However, recognizing this as a right also means recognizing the government's responsibility to deliver it properly. There can be no room for substandard food, irregular supplies, wastage, or corruption.
Thus, the minister's warning that poor-quality or unsuitable food will not be accepted is welcome.
Transparency and accountability must be built into every stage of the program, from procurement and transportation to distribution at individual schools. Teachers, parents and local communities should have meaningful avenues to monitor what children are receiving, and report irregularities.
Most importantly, the program must be expanded carefully and sustainably so that children across the country, regardless of where they live or their family's financial circumstances, can benefit.
A midday meal should never be something a child has to feel grateful for. It is an investment in their health, education and future -- and, by extension, in Bangladesh's future.

item.title: The power of thinking and questioning. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
More than three centuries ago, French philosopher René Descartes coined the famous phrase Cogito, ergo sum (I think, therefore I am) to define the essence of human existence.
His statement suggests that our ability to think is what makes us conscious, aware, and uniquely human. Because of the ability to think, human beings are often regarded as the most intelligent creatures on Earth.
Yet an important question remains: How many of us truly think, and how many think effectively?
In today's fast-paced world, there is a fine line between thinking and overthinking. Unfortunately, whenever someone pauses to analyze an issue deeply, question assumptions, or explore different possibilities, they are often labeled an “overthinker.”
As a result, many people become hesitant to ask questions or challenge conventional ideas.
However, progress has never come from unquestioned acceptance. Every invention, discovery, and social transformation began when someone dared to think differently and ask a simple but powerful question: “Why?”
Innovation is not merely about creating new technology; it is about developing new ways of understanding and solving problems. In a world facing increasingly complex challenges, the ability to think critically and question intelligently is a necessity.
If we look around Bangladesh, we will find no shortage of crises.
Every monsoon, floods affect millions of people, disrupting education, livelihoods, and communication.
In our cities, traffic congestion consumes valuable hours that could otherwise be spent on productive activities.
Plastic waste blocks drainage systems, contributing to urban flooding, while environmental pollution continues to threaten public health.
These problems are often discussed, criticized, and debated. Yet meaningful solutions emerge only when people move beyond complaints and begin asking the right questions.
Take the issue of urban flooding. Instead of merely blaming heavy rainfall, an innovative mind asks: Why do roads remain submerged long after the rain stops? Are drainage systems inadequate? Is unmanaged waste preventing water from flowing properly?
Such questions encourage us to investigate root causes rather than visible symptoms. Once the causes are identified, practical solutions become easier to design, whether through improved waste management, better urban planning, or community awareness campaigns.
Similarly, traffic congestion is not simply a transportation problem; it is also a thinking problem.
Every day, thousands of people lose valuable time on the roads. But what if students, engineers, and policy-makers worked together to rethink public transportation? What if technology could be used to monitor traffic flow more efficiently? What if flexible working hours reduced rush-hour pressure?
Progress begins when people challenge the assumption that existing conditions are unavoidable.
The same principle applies to education. Many students in remote areas still face barriers to quality learning. Rather than accepting this reality, innovators ask how digital technologies, community-based learning initiatives, or low-cost educational resources can bridge the gap.
Every educational advancement begins with someone identifying a problem and refusing to believe that it cannot be solved.
Innovation is not limited to laboratories, scientists, or large corporations. It begins with observation. It grows through curiosity. It develops through questioning.
A student who wonders how to reduce food waste in the cafeteria, save electricity in classrooms, or improve the campus environment is already thinking like an innovator.
The goal is not simply to find answers but to cultivate the habit of asking meaningful questions.
As Bangladesh moves toward a future shaped by rapid technological advancement and global challenges, the country will need more than skilled workers. It will need critical thinkers, problem-solvers, and innovators.
The next breakthrough idea may not come from a famous inventor or a multinational company. It may come from a student who dares to ask a question that others overlook.
Thinking is not a luxury but a responsibility. Questioning is not a sign of weakness but the beginning of wisdom. Every crisis carries within it an opportunity for innovation.
The moment we stop accepting problems as permanent and start questioning them, we take the first step toward meaningful change.
After all, every great solution begins with a simple question: “What if there is a better way?”
Md Inzamul Haque is a lecturer at the Department of English, Southeast University.

item.title: On the road again. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Travel has lost some of its old appeal in the global age, aided by instantaneous internet communication and the relative ease of travelling long distances.
In the old days, travel had a special meaning, particularly when the destination was a faraway country and the journey itself involved flying across continents.
Globalization, we are told, has killed distance. These days, hardly any place seems truly far away. Internet-mediated communication has also, in a sense, diminished culture shock.
Whether viscerally, in person, or virtually, we have already seen so much of the world. We can watch its streets, its people, its food, its politics and its landscapes on our screens.
Yet travelogue is not dead yet.
It is the unexpected encounters and experiences for which we are rarely prepared that make travelling worthwhile.
Zadar: Where nature plays music
In Zadar, an ancient Croatian city on the Adriatic coast, we encountered something that could hardly be experienced through a computer screen: The Sea Organ.
Built into the waterfront, it produces music through the movement of the waves. The sea itself becomes the musician.
As the waves enter the organ's pipes, they generate sounds that rise and fall unpredictably. Nearby, the Sun Salutation -- another remarkable installation -- responds to sunlight with a different kind of spectacle.
Between the sea, the sunset and the installations, Zadar offers something close to a symphony of nature and human creativity.
The waves of the Adriatic not only catch the eye; they soothe the ear.
That is perhaps what travel does best. It brings together things that we may know intellectually but have never actually experienced.
Education, sport, and Croatia
We attended a workshop at the University of Zadar, an institution that goes back to 1396, one of the oldest universities in East Europe.
Later, we met members of the city council. Their offices were decorated with large posters of famous Croatian football stars. It was football season, and the national team was very much on people's minds.
I asked a simple question: How does a country of fewer than four million people repeatedly produce athletes capable of competing at the highest level of international sport?
Football, of course, is only part of the story. Croatia has also produced world-class athletes in tennis, skiing, rowing, water polo, handball, athletics, and other sports. The country's sporting achievements are remarkable relative to its small population.
Sport is taken seriously as part of children's education and community life. Croatia has a national sports program that explicitly links sport with the educational system and sets responsibilities for national and local authorities, while its education system includes physical education and opportunities for students to pursue sport more intensively.
The idea that education, sport, music, and community life could be treated as complementary components of a child's development struck me.
Migrants far from home
Croatia also has experienced a significant increase in foreign workers, including workers from Nepal who are quite visible. Bangladeshis were present too though in much smaller numbers.
I had conversations with Bangladeshi workers in Malaysia during their work breaks. They seemed pleasantly surprised that people they described as bhadralok -- people from the educated and relatively privileged sections of society -- would simply stop and talk to them on the sidewalk.
Many described precarious lives: Insecure employment, uncertain immigration status, and limited social support.
One worker told me something that stayed with me. When ministers and senior officials from Dhaka visited Malaysia, he said, they often met Bengali businesspeople, community leaders, and embassy officials but had little time to meet the ordinary workers whose remittances make such an important contribution to Bangladesh's economy.
I wondered: Why should it be so difficult to talk to the people who do some of the hardest work and whose earnings contribute so substantially to the country's foreign-exchange reserves?
Perhaps governments everywhere need to remember that migrants are not merely sources of remittances. They are citizens, workers, and human beings whose experiences provide an important measure of how a country values its people.
Australia: Democracy and the welfare state
In Australia, I spent some quiet time at the Museum of Australian Democracy at Old Parliament House in Canberra.
The building was Australia's federal Parliament from 1927 until 1988, when Parliament moved to the new Parliament House on Capital Hill. In 2009, the old building became the home of the Museum of Australian Democracy.
Walking through the museum was an encounter with Australia's political memory. I came across displays devoted to former prime ministers, including references to their education and careers.
Among them was Robert -- Bob -- Hawke, whom I had briefly encountered in Adelaide in 2015. Hawke, then in a wheelchair, appeared at a conference I was attending. He came to our session, and I had the opportunity to shake his hand and exchange a few words with him.
When I met him, I reminded him that I had been a graduate student in the United States when he became prime minister and had read about his life in The New York Times. That was how I knew about his Rhodes Scholarship.
He seemed pleased that I remembered it. But I had the impression that, for Hawke, being a Rhodes Scholar was not what defined his life.
His real accomplishments, in his own eyes, were his leadership of the trade union movement and his service as prime minister.
That distinction is worth remembering. Education can open doors, but what a person does with that education is ultimately more important than the credential itself.
Australia also offers an interesting example of the welfare state in everyday life.
Habibul Haque Khondker is a sociologist and columnist.

item.title: Ninth national pay scale: The real test. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Public employees deserve fair wages. But a government pay scale is never only about government employees.
When millions of households are already struggling with high prices, weak purchasing power, and economic uncertainty, a large public-sector wage increase inevitably becomes a question of wider economic justice.
That is why the approval of the ninth national pay scale deserves to be examined not simply as a salary revision, but as a major macro-economic policy decision.
The new pay structure raises basic salaries by up to 142%, with the minimum basic salary rising to Tk20,000 and the maximum to Tk1,56,000. Full implementation is expected to require an additional Tk106,000 crore annually.
The question is not whether government employees deserve better pay. They do. The harder question is: How can Bangladesh implement such a large wage adjustment without making life even more expensive for everyone else?
Bangladesh is entering this reform with little room for complacency. Headline inflation stood at 8.32% in July 2026, while non-food inflation remained higher at 9.28%. The average inflation rate for FY2025–26 was 8.68%.
For a salaried household, these numbers are not abstract economic indicators. They mean that the same income buys less food, transport, education, healthcare, and other necessities than it did before.
And the burden is not evenly distributed.
According to the latest Labour Force Survey 2024, around 84% of employed people -- approximately 5.80 crore workers -- are engaged in informal employment.
These workers do not receive a government pay revision every few years. Many have no automatic cost-of-living adjustment, no guaranteed annual increment, and limited protection against sudden price increases.
This creates the central distributional dilemma of pay scale: A wage increase for millions of public employees can be justified, but who protects the millions who have no employer capable of passing higher costs on to someone else?
Of course, the pay scale alone will not cause Bangladesh’s inflation. That would be economically simplistic. Inflation has multiple drivers -- exchange rates, food supply, import costs, energy prices, market concentration, fiscal and monetary conditions, and global commodity shocks.
But a major wage-driven increase in aggregate demand can add pressure when supply-side constraints are already severe.
The transmission mechanism is straightforward:
Government wages rise → consumption rises → prices respond → private employees demand higher wages → business costs increase → investment and competitiveness suffer → inflationary pressure persists.
This concern is not simply theoretical. Business leaders have already warned that higher public-sector wages could increase pressure on the private sector, particularly labour-intensive industries already struggling with energy shortages, high borrowing costs, and an unstable business environment.
If private employers respond by raising wages, they may also face higher production costs. If they cannot absorb those costs, prices may rise. If they cannot raise prices because of weak demand or international competition, investment and employment may suffer.
This is where Bangladesh needs to look beyond the government payroll.
The latest external economic outlook is hardly reassuring. The World Bank has projected Bangladesh’s FY2025–26 growth at only 3.9%, citing elevated inflation, weak investment, financial-sector vulnerabilities, and the effects of the Middle East conflict.
It has also warned that poverty has already increased and that further shocks could push more people below the poverty line.
Recent shocks have pushed up international prices of energy and agricultural inputs, with crude oil, LNG, and nitrogen fertilizer prices all experiencing significant increases.
For Bangladesh, this matters enormously. Higher energy and fertilizer costs eventually reach farmers, transport operators, manufacturers, and consumers.
The agricultural economy is particularly vulnerable. According to FAO, around 10 lakh agricultural households -- nearly 50 lakh people -- are projected to need emergency agricultural assistance during June-November 2026.
These numbers should force a broader question: While the state increases the purchasing power of public employees, what is the state’s plan for protecting the purchasing power of everyone else?
At present, Bangladesh’s social safety-net system is not designed to function as a universal shield against inflation. Informal workers, low-income households, small producers, and many private-sector employees remain highly exposed to economic shocks.
A pay scale without a parallel protection strategy risks creating a two-speed economy: One group receives an institutionalized income adjustment, while another absorbs the consequences through higher prices and weaker real wages.
That would be economically inefficient and socially unfair.
What should be done?
First, establish a pay scale-inflation monitoring framework. The government should monitor the impact of the new pay structure on inflation, consumption, private-sector wages, employment, and fiscal sustainability.
If inflationary pressures intensify significantly, subsequent phases of implementation should be reviewed rather than treated as automatic.
Second, protect workers beyond the public payroll. Temporary, targeted income support should be expanded for low-income informal workers and vulnerable households during periods of severe inflation. Social protection must become more responsive to economic shocks rather than functioning mainly as a collection of static programs.
Third, address the supply side. Wage reform cannot be separated from food security, energy reliability, fertilizer availability, import management, and market competition. If supply cannot respond to rising demand, wage increases will translate too easily into higher prices.
Fourth, finance the pay scale through structural reform rather than excessive fiscal pressure. Stronger domestic revenue mobilization, better tax compliance, expenditure rationalization, and improved public financial management are essential. Borrowing simply to finance recurrent wage and pension commitments would shift today's adjustment costs onto tomorrow's taxpayers.
Finally, Bangladesh must stop viewing wage policy, inflation policy, and social protection as separate policy silos. They are deeply interconnected.
A government employee struggling to pay rent and educate children deserves a decent salary.
But so does the garment worker whose wage does not automatically rise with inflation.
So does the rickshaw puller whose daily income is uncertain.
So does the small farmer face higher fertilizer and fuel costs.
So does the informal worker who has no pension, no paid leave, and no protection against economic shocks.
The real measure of the ninth national pay scale should therefore not be how much government employees receive on their pay slips. It should be whether Bangladesh can raise public-sector incomes without reducing the real incomes of millions outside the public sector.
The government has an opportunity to demonstrate that wage reform and economic stability do not have to be opposing goals. But that needs more than a new salary structure.
It requires a coherent macroeconomic strategy that manages inflation, protects vulnerable workers, strengthens supply chains, and ensures that fiscal reform is sustainable.
A pay rise for some should not become a price rise for everyone. That is the real test.
Amith Kumar Malaker is a human rights defender and public policy analyst based in Bangladesh.

New York's Muslims reclaim their city 25 years after 9/11 attacks. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Asad Dandia was eight when he watched the Sept 11, 2001 attacks on television at his Pakistani-immigrant parents’ home in New York.

Then came the backlash — years of Islamophobia as Americans processed attacks that had killed nearly 3,000 people.

There was anger, suspicion and worse.

At 19, Dandia experienced a police informant posing as a friend to infiltrate his family home, part of a now-disgraced surveillance effort purportedly seeking to detect extremism.

Today, though, the 33-year-old historian finds a New York transformed: one with its first Muslim mayor, public prayers in Times Square and new mosques rising across the city.

“Twenty-five years after 9/11, we mourn and we grieve what happened, and at the same time, we recognise that I am not responsible for what happened,” he told AFP.

“I don’t deserve to be targeted for what happened, and I am as much of a New Yorker as anybody else in that respect,” said Dandia, who leads walking tours centred on the city’s Muslim communities.

Islamophobia surged in the United States after the 2001 attacks in which militants hijacked airliners and flew them into Manhattan’s World Trade Centre and the Pentagon outside Washington. A fourth plane crashed into a Pennsylvania field after a passenger revolt.

Muslims reported increased public assaults and harassment, and some stopped wearing visual markers such as hijabs in a bid to conceal their religion.

Meanwhile, US authorities monitored Muslims by requiring thousands of men and boys to register with the government, leading to many being deported from the country.

“Everyone was in such fear,” said Mohammed Razvi, a native Pakistani who founded the Council of Peoples Organisation non-profit to support Muslims in New York after 9/11.

“We had gunshots fired in our neighbourhood by individuals who felt that we were responsible,” he added.

Razvi said he started introducing himself as “Mo” after 9/11 to avoid the stigma he encountered when saying “Mohammad”.

“Muslims trying to live the American dream were being blamed for something they had nothing to do with or even control,” he said.

‘Terrifying’

In New York, police began surveilling hundreds of Muslims as part of their counterterrorism strategy, often targeting people without evidence of wrongdoing.

Dandia experienced this as a 19-year-old college student, when a young Bangladeshi man joined a mutual aid charity he had started.

The pair grew close: sharing meals, playing sports and even sleeping at Dandia’s home. But seven months later, the man revealed that he was an NYPD informant sent to monitor Dandia and his community.

“It was heartbreaking, but it was also terrifying,” he recalled. “My relationship with the world around me shifted underneath my feet.”

After his ordeal, Dandia and rights groups won a landmark legal settlement that restricted the NYPD from launching similar surveillance programmes and established a watchdog to monitor the force.

For Gadier Abbas, an attorney with the Council on American-Islamic Relations, the NYPD programme was the prime example of the “anti-Muslim hysteria” that followed 9/11.

But today, Abbas said, “there is a lot of hope”.

“You see American Muslims in every single walk of life, almost at every single level, and that’s a testament to the vibrancy of the community.”

‘Power’

New York will soon boast the largest mosque in the state — one of more than 100 added since 2001 in New York — while Muslims are a rising cultural and political force.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who took his oath of office on the Holy Quran, has become the new face of American leftist politics.

Still, Islamophobia persists in the city where around nine per cent of the population is Muslim.

In March, a far-right influencer organised a “Stop the Islamic Takeover of New York City” rally outside the mayor’s residence.

Meanwhile, a conservative senator has said Mamdani should be sent to Guantanamo Bay, the US detention camp best known for holding 9/11 suspects.

Some relatives of September 11 victims have called for Mamdani — an avid supporter of Palestinian rights — to skip this year’s 9/11 memorial, while other families have defended the mayor.

Dandia acknowledged Islamophobia had not disappeared, but he was optimistic about how far New York’s Muslim community has come.

“I’ve seen the growth of our institutional power, but also the recognition by other New Yorkers who are not Muslim, that we are all part of this city together,” he said.

“I think that’s really valuable because, you know, Rome was not built overnight, and it was not built by one person or one group of people. It was built by the community.”

item.title: Addressing safety in the country. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The growing circulation of illegal firearms across Bangladesh is becoming a threat that can no longer be treated as merely another law-and-order concern.
At a time when public confidence in safety is already under considerable pressure, the proliferation of guns and the rise in firearm-related killings make the need for effective state action greater than ever.
According to police records, at least 123 shooting incidents occurred across the country in the first seven months of this year, leaving more than 50 people dead. More alarming still, 1,311 weapons -- including rifles and submachine guns -- looted from police facilities during the August 2024 unrest and more than 257,000 rounds of ammunition also remain missing.
These figures should be a wake-up call. Illegal firearms are being used in political clashes, territorial disputes, drug-related conflicts, extortion, and criminal rivalries.
Ordinary citizens inevitably become vulnerable when such violence spills into public spaces, and people should not have to wonder whether a political confrontation, neighbourhood dispute, or criminal feud could suddenly put their lives at risk.
While the government's formation of a special unit to recover looted and illegal firearms is a welcome, albeit belated, step, it must be accompanied by sustained and measurable action.
Recovering the weapons already outside state control must be an urgent priority, while intelligence and law enforcement agencies need to identify and dismantle the networks bringing new firearms into the country.
Most importantly, enforcement cannot be selective. Political affiliation, criminal influence, or social standing must not determine who is investigated or prosecuted.
The public has a fundamental right to safety. The government must step up now -- not simply to respond to individual shootings, but to prevent the country from becoming increasingly accustomed to armed violence.

item.title: We are killing our rivers. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The latest survey from Bangladesh Inland Water Transport Authority (BIWTA) on water pollution in Dhaka is nothing short of shocking: 424 outlets are dumping an estimated 330 tons of waste every single day into the Buriganga, Turag, Balu, and Shitalakkhya rivers around Dhaka.
To reduce this to mismanagement and oversight is no longer possible and must be called what it is -- environmental negligence on a staggering scale.
When a nation’s lifelines are treated as open sewers, the consequences are inevitable: Toxic water, collapsing ecosystems, public health crises, and a future that becomes harder to salvage with each passing year.
That out of the 424 identified discharge points, 244 are linked to privately owned factories and industrial establishments, tells us of the impunity enjoyed by industries in our country, where they have felt emboldened to continue polluting our rivers and affect millions of lives.
This feeble enforcement and non-existent accountability needs to be addressed with immediate effect.
Let it be reiterated: Dhaka’s rivers are dying because the authorities responsible for protecting them have failed to act. All the mandates, budgets, and legal powers mean nothing if there is no urgency to do what is right for the people of this country.
When 330 tons of waste enter the water system daily, “monitoring” and “future plans” are meaningless. Only decisive action matters.
The respected authorities must literally clean up their act. While the long term plan must include proper sewage treatment and enforcing effluent treatment requirements without exception, there is an immediate need to prosecute violators and ensure that sewer lines are not secretly connected to rivers.
Bangladesh cannot aspire to economic transformation while its rivers remain toxic drains. The numbers in this survey are a national embarrassment and must be treated as a call to action. The authorities must prove they are willing to act, not just talk.

item.title: The next green revolution. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Bangladesh is entering one of the most critical periods in its agricultural history. Over the last five decades, the country achieved remarkable success in food production through irrigation expansion, high-yielding varieties, fertilizer use, and the hard work of millions of farmers. From a food-deficit nation after independence, Bangladesh has now become one of the world’s leading rice producers.
Yet the challenges ahead are enormous.
Climate change, shrinking cultivable land, labour shortages, rising production costs, groundwater depletion, salinity intrusion, floods, and increasing pest and disease pressure are threatening future food security. To sustain production for nearly 180 million people in the coming decades, Bangladesh must embrace a new scientific revolution in agriculture.
The future of Bangladeshi agriculture will likely be driven by biotechnology, artificial intelligence (AI), drones, precision agriculture, smart irrigation, robotics, and climate-smart farming systems.
Bangladesh produced an estimated 38 million tons of rice in 2025, according to FAO forecasts, largely driven by strong Boro and Aman harvests. item.title: If nothing changes, then nothing changes. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
This past week, a city neighbourhood witnessed a violent turf war for control of the illicit drug trade. Several people sustained gunshot wounds, though, fortunately, no one was killed.
An initial probe found politically-linked drug dealers behind the violence, with the clashes apparently driven entirely by the desire to secure territory under a new political settlement.
Only a couple of weeks ago, this paper ran a report detailing how trucks carrying fruit to the city’s prime trading hub were caught in a web of extortion. Truck drivers at Dhaka’s Badamtoli riverfront wholesale fruit market face systematic extortion by an illegal syndicate that uses government-authorized parking arrangements as a front.
Operators are charged more than 20 times the official parking fee simply to access the area, with a local ruling-party leader accused of directing the unauthorized collections.
Meanwhile, Shahed Sharif, a teenager, created a website named “ghush.site” late last month to protest the constant demands for bribes he faced while trying to withdraw his late schoolteacher mother’s pension.
Numerous citizens have since shared their own grievances on the platform. Up until the afternoon of September 1, a total of 11,666 complaints had been submitted to Shahed’s bribe-tracking site, with the total amount demanded reaching more than Tk357 crore.
In addition, recent surprise visits by high-ranking government officials to hospitals and land offices have revealed the dismal state of public services, with too many staff members remaining willfully absent.
All these examples speak poorly of the state of affairs in post-Monsoon Revolution Bangladesh. Aspirations were high -- not only to get rid of an authoritarian regime but also to witness a qualitative change in the country. Yet, if nothing changes, then nothing changes.
Though currently in a very difficult position, citizens can still endure the energy crisis if they receive a credible assurance from the government that efforts are underway to provide respite from gas shortages and electricity load-shedding.
These are not systemic failures per se; they can be addressed with the right steps. But when it comes to the quality of public life, certain things matter far more.
If your neighbourhood is not yet safe for your sons and daughters to move around in, and if dens of drug dealers remain operational, what change are we talking about?
If fruit vendors charge you more for every apple you buy on the “genuine” excuse that political elements have inflated prices through illicit extortion, what change are we talking about?
If institution after institution remains infested with bribery rackets, what public services can citizens expect from a “changed Bangladesh?”
In some recent heinous crime cases, law enforcers managed to apprehend the “criminals” very promptly. But when public suspicion runs high over the authenticity of those “captures,” it speaks volumes about the growing distrust of state institutions.
This is not a sign of a healthy democracy. It is a testament to the fact that, long after the changeover, we still have not managed to rebuild institutions that have long lacked transparency and accountability.
One no longer needs Transparency International or other social barometers to publish annual corruption reports on Bangladesh; citizens are literally living through graft in their daily lives.
Shahed Sharif’s website is just one glaring example of how corruption has become all-pervasive in a society where public offices are not yet held accountable.
At the level of state governance, it is well understood that until an aggressive catalyst alters legislative, electoral, or structural inputs, systemic inertia keeps public policies, economic trajectories, and institutional cultures stagnant.
Regime change by default does not make a substantive difference unless the political leadership embodies that change.
Over the years, the political system has been structured in a way that blurs the line between the government and the ruling party.
Power elites quickly become preoccupied with appeasing a large number of beneficiaries who manage to secure positions on one party front or another.
Consequently, undue advantages in work contracts, illicit toll collections, and the drug trade become inherent to the system.
With every change of guard, one group of politicians and their sidekicks simply replaces the old beneficiaries, while ordinary people -- the main stakeholders -- are forced to take a back seat.
As a result, citizens rarely see a tangible difference in their everyday lives. They still have to navigate the open trade of illicit drugs in their neighbourhoods, unsafe roads, illegal tolls in marketplaces, and bribery for every service they are entitled to as citizens of Bangladesh.
Governments often become trapped in cycles of compounding stagnation and the status quo because their primary motivation is catering to a narrow constituency: Party leaders and cadres.
In the process, they become oblivious to the everyday challenges faced by the wider population in a democracy.
When institutions remain weak and public offices fail to provide due services, entrenched special interest groups, lobbyists, and party cadres optimize their profits from the entire state system.
Reaz Ahmad is Editor, Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: Before the Earth moves. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The earthquake tragedy in Colombia last month should make Bangladesh ask a question that has little to do with predicting earthquakes: What happens when most of a nation's population, opportunity, and institutional capacity become concentrated in one city?
The United Nations projects Dhaka to become the world's largest city by 2050, with a population exceeding 50 million. Bangladesh already struggles with congestion, housing shortages, groundwater stress, pollution, inadequate sanitation, and enormous pressure on public services. Add tens of millions of people to this urban system, and earthquake vulnerability becomes only one dimension of a much larger human-development challenge.
Bangladesh already has projects designed to strengthen secondary cities, transportation corridors, and areas outside Dhaka. But the scale of the coming transformation requires something larger.
We should stop thinking primarily about moving people and start moving opportunities.
Start with those whose jobs may not survive
Walk through Dhaka and one sees an extraordinary amount of human effort.
A rickshaw puller pedals through extreme heat. A day labourer waits each morning hoping someone needs him. A young graduate rides a bicycle for deliveries because he cannot find work matching his education. A garment worker wonders whether automation will eventually replace part of her job. A rural worker leaves home because Dhaka appears to offer the only realistic path toward higher income.
These people are often described statistically as “labour.”
They are something much more important: Bangladesh's human capital.
The question is whether Bangladesh will continue using millions of people in occupations producing relatively little economic value and offering limited upward mobility or invest in enabling those same people to build the next economy.
Consider the rickshaw puller. The policy objective should not be to ban his rickshaw. That simply destroys income.
Ask instead: What could this person be doing 10 years from now?
Could he become a construction technician? A plumber? A logistics worker? A solar installer? A water-treatment operator? An emergency-response worker?
Then ask the more important question: What would it take to get him there?
That is human development.
Bangladesh may need housing and infrastructure for tens of millions of additional urban residents over the coming decades.
That sounds like a burden. It could also represent one of the largest employment opportunities in the country's history.
Building a network of 20 or 30 major economic centres would require enormous numbers of electricians, plumbers, welders, machine operators, construction workers, engineers, drivers, healthcare workers, water technicians, teachers, maintenance workers, and logistics professionals, among countless others.
Bangladesh already has much of the labour. The challenge is transforming skills.
Imagine a national program under which workers in vulnerable or low-productivity occupations receive paid training for three to 12 months. Training would be tied directly to employment.
The worker would not receive a certificate and then be told to search for a job. Infrastructure contracts receiving public support would commit to hiring qualified graduates.
The pathway becomes: Informal work → training → skilled employment → stable income → housing → financial inclusion → family security.
Urbanization then becomes a mechanism for social mobility.
Don't build another Dhaka
The objective should not be to create another megacity containing 30 million people.
Bangladesh needs a network.
Imagine economic centres distributed along existing and future rail, highway, and river corridors.
Some could specialize in healthcare and pharmaceuticals. Others in advanced textiles, food processing, logistics, electronics, renewable energy, technology, or light manufacturing.
Each would combine employment with housing, hospitals, schools, universities, parks, public transportation, and digital infrastructure.
That distinction is essential.
People do not move because planners draw circles on maps. They move because they can build better lives.
A family will leave Dhaka voluntarily when another city offers a good job, affordable home, safe school, reliable hospital, clean water, and reasonable transportation.
Bangladesh should therefore not attempt to redistribute population. It should redistribute reasons for people to choose where they live.
Water must come before homes
Water security should determine where these new centres grow.
Dhaka illustrates what happens when population growth outruns environmental infrastructure. The World Bank's current Metro Dhaka Water Security and Resilience Program describes serious pollution of rivers and canals resulting from rapid urbanization, inadequate sanitation, industrial discharge, and waste.
Bangladesh cannot sustainably replicate this pattern across the country. The next generation of cities should reverse the sequence.
Before approving hundreds of thousands of apartments, establish where their water will come from. Protect wetlands. Build reservoirs. Capture rainwater. Treat sewage. Recycle wastewater for industry. Protect groundwater recharge. Separate stormwater from sewage. Monitor industrial discharge digitally.
Bangladesh is one of the most water-rich landscapes on Earth, yet millions of citizens still experience problems involving safe drinking water.
That paradox demonstrates that water security is not merely about how much water a country possesses. It is about whether infrastructure delivers clean water to people when and where they need it.
Urban policy is health policy
The benefits would extend directly into national health.
A hospital treats disease after it occurs. A well-designed city can prevent some disease before the patient reaches the hospital.
Clean water reduces waterborne illness. Modern sanitation reduces exposure to pathogens. Cleaner transportation improves air quality. Better drainage reduces stagnant contaminated water. Trees and shaded streets reduce dangerous heat exposure. Walkable communities encourage physical activity. Shorter commutes give parents more time to their children. Formal employment makes health insurance and retirement savings more achievable. Distributed medical centres reduce the need for families across Bangladesh to travel to Dhaka for treatment.
For a country with limited healthcare resources, prevention through better living conditions may be among the highest-return health investments available.
Then there is the earthquake.
The magnitude-7.4 earthquake that struck Colombia last month demonstrated again how quickly buildings, roads, and ordinary lives can be transformed by seismic disaster.
Bangladesh cannot know exactly when a major earthquake will strike the region. But Dhaka's vulnerability is well documented.
The answer cannot simply be more ambulances and rescue equipment.
If tens of millions of people, major hospitals, government institutions, financial organizations, and businesses remain concentrated within the same metropolitan region, Bangladesh is effectively concentrating national risk.
Developing multiple economic centres is therefore similar to diversifying an investment portfolio. If one region suffers catastrophe, the country continues functioning. Decentralization becomes national insurance.
Give Dhaka room to breathe
This strategy does not require abandoning Dhaka. It may be the best way to save it.
As future population growth increasingly occurs elsewhere, Dhaka can begin repairing the damage created by decades of uncontrolled expansion.
Unsafe buildings can gradually be replaced. Canals can be restored. Wetlands can be protected. Emergency roads can be widened. Schools and hospitals can be retrofitted. Waterways can again become environmental assets rather than drains.
Dhaka could become safer without becoming economically irrelevant.
The objective is not to weaken Dhaka. It is to make Bangladesh stronger than Dhaka alone.
Dr Mazher Mir is a Bangladeshi writer with over three decades of work on socio-economic and human development issues.
